<reason>CON (A) was the more vivid and aggressive debater: the "PRO's model is my model plus a fee" reframe, the lever argument (fee hits the courier, not the receiver), and the "exit dressed as efficiency" florist line were sharp and narrowed the debate. But PRO (B) held the motion's actual decision rule—cities "should be allowed" to use the tool—and neutralized CON's central fairness claim: a free curb also rations by capacity to absorb cost, just hidden in lost working time, and the florist's single immobilized van is hurt more by a queue than a fleet is. CON's reply (the florist simply exits) was asserted rather than shown. PRO also defused the "not really dynamic" semantic attack (CON conceded "the label was never the problem"), and correctly pointed out CON's inelastic-core premise was an assumption that one fixed stop cannot prove; platform-level consolidation remained a live mechanism. CON over-read PRO's conditional concessions and had its second rebuttal clipped. CON dropped the pass-through-to-vulnerable-riders line after PRO's off-peak answer. Close, but PRO left fewer burdens unanswered on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The florist exchange: CON's "time is the one currency the small operator holds at par" was met by PRO's "confuses equal minutes with equal burdens"—ten minutes idling a florist's only van is not ten minutes spread across a fleet, so a free curb already sorts by resources. This flipped CON's strongest fairness frame and CON's "she stops coming" reply was speculative rather than demonstrated.</best_rebuttal>
